then.text: Double Gloucester, cloth-bound, turned every day. It's the colour of a good sunset and goes with everything except a diet.

The 'double' means a double-size wheel, made from full-cream milk, so it matures into a rich, nutty cheese. The orange colour was originally added so that it looked like the richer cheese. Annatto. It's from a seed.
Off you go to the Master. And do me a favour: let the cheese win now and then. It's good for its self-esteem.
Look at that! A Gloucelet, round as a good wheel and twice as stubborn. It is, as far as anyone knows, made of mostly cheese and a bit of attitude.
Right. You're ready. The Master's waiting at the top of the hill.

else.text: You need to have a Gloucelet to show first. They live in the tall grass on the wold and on the hill. Look for something round, orange and furious. It rolls when it's cross.

then.text: The rules of the race? Easy. There aren't any. A round of Double Gloucester, about three to four kilos in a wooden case, is launched at the top; it gets a start, and everyone follows. First to the bottom wins the cheese.
Nobody catches the cheese. It moves faster than a car on a motorway. The winner is the one who crosses the line first, which is usually the one who didn't fall over.
Now, the creature version. You'll need a Gloucelet: the wheel of Double Gloucester that learned to roll for itself. Catch one on the hill or the wold and show me.

else.text: Cooper's Hill Dairy. Double Gloucester made as it was in the vale: full-cream milk, a cloth, a press and patience.
If you're after the cheese-rolling, the Master of Ceremonies is at the top of the hill.

cw_dairyshop.text: We make the wheels, then we turn them every day for weeks. If we stop turning, the rind goes wrong. There's a rhyme: turn it, brush it, leave it alone. I don't remember the rest, I've been turning.
A Double Gloucester that's rolled down Cooper's Hill is never for eating. They use a lookalike wheel for the race, and a lovely real one for the winner.
